entries.clue: Son, clumsy, far from alert (10)

annotation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a son who is both clumsy and dozy.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make it read as a list of a boy's faults; in fact the first two items build the answer and the third defines it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sleeper is unconscious, the opposite of alert.

entries.clue: Git given a fizzy drink (4)

blocks.note: git and sod are both British insults for an unpleasant person

annotation.surface: Someone unpleasant is handed a fizzy drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Git and sod are mild British terms of abuse for an annoying man.
annotation.definitionFit: Soda is carbonated water, the standard fizzy drink.

entries.clue: Regularly unteach Mormons found in this state (4)

indicatorNotes.Regularly: at regular intervals: take every other letter

annotation.surface: A hint that missionaries in some state are unlearning their teaching.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue: Utah is the state most associated with the Mormon church, whose headquarters are in Salt Lake City.
annotation.definitionFit: Utah was settled by Mormons and is still the centre of the Latter-day Saint church.

entries.clue: Sweet book with Sussex setting … (8,4)

blocks.note: a stick of rock sold at a Sussex seaside resort
Graham Greene's 1938 novel, set on the Sussex coast

annotation.surface: A description of a novel set in southern England.
annotation.walkthrough: Rock is a hard, cylindrical British seaside sweet with the resort's name running through it; Brighton is a resort in Sussex. The ellipsis carries the answer into 4 down.
annotation.definitionFit: Brighton rock is both the seaside sweet and the title of Greene's Brighton-set novel.

entries.clue: … agreed, that’s an extract from it (5,2)

indicatorNotes.an extract from: an extract is a passage lifted out of a longer text, so the answer is lifted out of the middle of 'it'

blocks.note: 'it' is the answer to 3 down; drop its first letter and its last four

annotation.surface: Continuing 3 down: a reader agrees that a passage comes from the novel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' points back across the ellipsis to 3 down, so the letters sit inside that answer, b-RIGHT ON-rock, not inside this clue.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the exclamation 'right on!' voices hearty agreement.

entries.clue: Safari centre sees Everyman fatigue abrupt Scotsman after capsizing (7)

indicatorNotes.abrupt: cut short: the last letter of bore is lopped off
indicatorNotes.after capsizing: capsizing turns a boat upside down; in a down clue the assembled letters are turned over, bottom to top

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I
bore = fatigue, weary; cut short to BOR
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

annotation.surface: A travelling Scotsman collapses from exhaustion somewhere on safari.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself in a clue usually means I or ME. Nairobi, Kenya's capital, is the usual starting point for East African safaris.
annotation.definitionFit: Nairobi is where most Kenyan safaris begin.

entries.clue: Possesseth headgear, ‘tis put on horse (4)

blocks.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

annotation.surface: Olde-worlde talk about putting a hat on a horse.
annotation.walkthrough: The archaic -eth of the definition asks for an archaic answer, and 'tis keeps the period flavour.
annotation.definitionFit: Hath is the old third-person form of has, just as possesseth is of possesses.

entries.clue: Accepting only some commands of orthodontists etc (3,2,5)

indicatorNotes.Accepting only some: take only some of the letters that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'commands', through 'of', into the start of 'orthodontists'

annotation.surface: A patient who follows only some of the dentist's orders.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the abbreviation tacked on the end, which reads as a lazy close to the sentence. The answer spans comm-ANDS OF ORTH-odontists.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: etc stands for et cetera, Latin for 'and the rest'.

entries.clue: Fake some deaths where people might be living (10)

indicatorNotes.Fake: faked letters are forged into a new arrangement

annotation.surface: Someone faking deaths, perhaps an insurance fraud, in places where people live.
annotation.walkthrough: The contrast of deaths and living hides that the middle two words are simply the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A homestead is a house with its land, a place where people live.

entries.clue: Pulling wrestling move that binds (7,3)

annotation.definitionNote: 'that binds' stands for a noun, a thing that binds

blocks.note: a pin holds an opponent's shoulders to the mat

annotation.surface: A wrestler's hold that ties up the opponent.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one wrestling hold, but it splits after 'Pulling'. A drawing pin is the British name for a thumbtack.
annotation.definitionFit: A drawing pin fastens paper to a board, so it is a thing that binds.

entries.clue: First man to block America First (4)

blocks.note: its first letter, which the clue's closing word also puts first
to dam a river is to block it

annotation.surface: A political slogan and someone trying to stop it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'America First' looks like the slogan, but it gives A and says where A goes; 'First' does double duty with the definition's 'First'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: in Genesis, Adam is the first human God makes.

entries.clue: Shrinking baked good: it’ll keep you in shape (8,4)

annotation.surface: A diet tip about a baked treat that won't ruin your figure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shrinking' and 'keep you in shape' pull towards dieting; shrinking here means shy, and the shape is a tucked gymnastic one.
annotation.definitionFit: A backward roll is a gymnastic exercise, done tucked into a ball.

entries.clue: Angry Charlotte and King Edward’s unwanted issues (3,8)

blocks.note: Charlotte and King Edward are British potato varieties

annotation.surface: A cross Charlotte and a king with problems nobody wants.
annotation.walkthrough: Charlotte and King Edward read as royalty, but both are potato varieties sold in British shops; together they are potatoes.
annotation.definitionFit: A hot potato is a controversial issue nobody wants to handle.

entries.clue: Director, light-hearted fellow, equips places with milkmaids (5,5)

annotation.surface: A cheerful film director kitting out rustic locations.
annotation.walkthrough: Four short pieces in clue order; the only trap is taking 'light-hearted fellow' as one person.
annotation.definitionFit: Milkmaids work where cows are milked, on dairy farms.

entries.clue: Inflamed, each lech’s mostly shown involuntary movement (10)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word: drop its last letter

blocks.note: a tic is an involuntary twitch

annotation.surface: A furious account of a lecherous man's twitching.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A pop' is informal for each, as in 'a pound a pop'.
annotation.definitionFit: Apoplectic means furious, inflamed with anger.

entries.clue: A long, powerful harmonic object rendered naturally, principally? (7)

annotation.definition: A long, powerful harmonic object rendered naturally, principally?

indicatorNotes.principally: take the principal, that is first, letters

blocks.clueFragment: A long, powerful harmonic object rendered naturally
blocks.note: the first letter of each of the seven words

annotation.surface: A description of a long horn played without valves.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue both spells the answer and describes it: an alphorn is a long wooden horn with no valves, so it plays only natural harmonics.
annotation.definitionFit: The alphorn is a very long, loud Alpine horn sounding the natural harmonic series.

entries.clue: Tedious far side of Stromboli, disruptive smoker (7)

indicatorNotes.far side of: the far end of the word, its last letter
indicatorNotes.disruptive: the letters are disrupted into a new order

annotation.surface: Complaining about a smoking volcano on a dreary stretch of coast.
annotation.walkthrough: Stromboli is a constantly erupting volcanic island off Sicily, so a 'smoker' there reads as the volcano, not the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Irksome means annoying and tiresome.

entries.clue: They describe pupils’ behaviour: explosions, gunshot, etc (7)

blocks.note: documents sent home at the end of a school term

annotation.surface: A teacher's note on unruly pupils, as if the classroom were a battlefield.
annotation.walkthrough: School reports are written assessments sent home to parents; a report is also the bang of a gun.
annotation.definitionFit: Reports are both school assessments and loud bangs.

entries.clue: Magnificent muesli in mix bachelor’s ingested (7)

indicatorNotes.in mix: the letters are put in a mix, scrambled
indicatorNotes.ingested: the bachelor's B is swallowed inside

blocks.note: B = bachelor, as in BA; it goes inside the mixed letters

annotation.surface: Praise for a muesli mix a single man has eaten.
annotation.walkthrough: Breakfast words make 'mix' and 'ingested' look like eating, but they are the two instructions.
annotation.definitionFit: Sublime means supremely fine, magnificent.

entries.clue: Ripped off like a dart (7)

annotation.surface: Robbed as sharply and quickly as a thrown dart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like a dart' reads as a simile for speed; it is literal, a dart being built with a shaft.
annotation.definitionFit: Shafted is slang for cheated or ripped off; a dart is shafted in having a shaft.

entries.clue: Poet, husky in voice? (7)

indicatorNotes.in voice: 'in voice' means as uttered by the voice, so the word is said, and what you hear is spelt differently

annotation.surface: Asking whether a poet has a rough voice.
annotation.walkthrough: Husky suggests a hoarse voice, but here it means covered in husks or shells, so shelly.
annotation.definitionFit: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English Romantic poet.

entries.clue: Euros for brioche? (6,5)

blocks.note: bread is slang for money, and euros are the money of France
a rich, buttery loaf from France

annotation.surface: Asking what you might pay for a brioche.
annotation.walkthrough: Bread is old slang for money, so the currency of France is literally French bread; the question mark flags the stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: Brioche is a type of loaf from France; euros are money in France, and bread is slang for money.

entries.clue: Miserable poet on the up (4)

indicatorNotes.on the up: in a down clue, going up means reading bottom to top

blocks.note: a bard is a poet, especially a Celtic one

annotation.surface: A gloomy poet whose fortunes are rising.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the up' sounds like improving prospects, at odds with 'Miserable'.
annotation.definitionFit: Drab means dull and cheerless.

entries.clue: Tennis legend showing evidence of fire and energy (4)

blocks.note: ash is what a fire leaves

annotation.surface: A tennis great playing with fire and energy.
annotation.walkthrough: Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975; 'fire and energy' reads as praise of his game.
annotation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was a champion American tennis player.

entries.clue: As delivered, proper ceremony (4)

indicatorNotes.As delivered: as a speech is delivered, spoken

annotation.surface: A formal ceremony performed correctly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As delivered' could mean as handed over; here it means as spoken.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a rite is a formal act performed as part of a ceremony.

entries.clue: Hoarding William’s canned food (10)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Hoarding' is singular in form; the answer is plural

indicatorNotes.canned: put in a can: one piece holds the other

blocks.note: board = meals, as in bed and board

annotation.surface: William stockpiling tinned food.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hoarding' reads as stockpiling, but it is the British word for a large advertising board, a billboard.
annotation.definitionFit: A hoarding is a billboard; the singular stands for the plural answer as a mass noun.

entries.clue: Nauseous, oily, not a little lugubrious (4)

indicatorNotes.not: 'not' negates, so the letter that follows is taken out of the word
indicatorNotes.a little: a little of the word, its first letter

blocks.note: slick = oily, as in an oil slick
first letter of lugubrious, removed from SLICK

annotation.surface: Feeling queasy and greasy, and more than a little gloomy.
annotation.walkthrough: Three adjectives look like a list of symptoms; only the first is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: nauseous describes the queasy feeling of being about to be ill.

entries.clue: ‘Cyber-’? ‘E-’? Call out what some junk may be! (10)

indicatorNotes.out: the letters are put out of order

annotation.surface: Puzzling over prefixes that tag things as online, then naming what junk might be.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and hyphens make 'Cyber-' and 'E-' look like prefixes to attach; they are just letters. 'Call out' reads as a phrase meaning shout.
annotation.definitionFit: Much household junk can be recycled.
